thread.title: Roku: It Wants to Be the Speaker of Your House

title: Roku: It Wants to Be the Speaker of Your House
text:
David Marino-Nachison July 16, 2018 1:09 p.m. ET
A lot of the Prime Day coverage is about Amazon.com ’s (AMZN) discounts on its Alexa devices , which are getting discounts that recall the price cuts it wielded around the holiday time to get truckloads of the talky little doodads into American homes.
But another Barron’s Next 50 company wants in on the action too: Roku (ROKU), which on Monday announced that it would launch a line of speakers meant to pair with Roku-enabled televisions. The speakers, now available for preorder, are listed at $200 but are currently on sale, natch. Newsletter Sign-up
The speakers are perhaps more Apple (AAPL) HomePod than Amazon Echo: In the announcement, Roku positioned them as high-powered audio devices rater than robot friends, saying they’re “meticulously engineered and calibrated to deliver powerful, premium” sound.
But they do come with a voice remote (as well as a tabletop one) that may help Roku device users get accustomed to conversations with their technology—and since Roku TVs come with audio apps, they might also induce users to keep them on, playing music as well as video programming. (The speakers are also Bluetooth-enabled.) More About Barron’s Next The Barron’s Next 50
Roku was once known mainly for its little video stick devices that plugged into TVs to offer up various bits of video software. It still does that, but its software also comes preinstalled on television sets, and its Roku Channel gives the company a free, add-supported, offering .
The company clearly faces stiff competition in streaming video, which makes its brand and technology extensions easy to understand. Meanwhile, one chief competitor, Netflix (NFLX), reports quarterly financial results after today’s market close . Roku shares are off about 7% in 2018, while FactSet’s mean analyst price target is slightly below current levels.
